sections.h2: Does Texas tax inheritances or estates?
sections.html:
Not anymore. Texas repealed its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752 (2015), effective September 1, 2015, which removed Tax Code Chapter 211.

The federal estate tax is the main death tax an heir hears about, and it reaches only large estates. For the heirs of a Texas house, the everyday issues are property tax, probate paperwork and recording the deed, all covered below.

sections.h2: When the federal estate tax applies
sections.html:
Form 706 comes into play only when the gross estate, adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption add up to more than the filing threshold for the year of death. Plain estates of cash, public securities and a few easily valued assets typically need no return.

Federal estate tax return filing thresholds by year of death
Year of deathFiling threshold
2020$11,580,000
2021$11,700,000
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Those amounts are filing triggers, not rates. For the estate, the house is valued at what it was worth on the date of death, not what the owner paid, and mortgages, debts, administration costs and gifts to a spouse or qualified charity come off the total. Spouses can elect portability of unused exemption by filing on time.

sections.h2: How the estate tax is figured
sections.html:
Federal tax is worked out in steps, and your house is just one line in the math. Texas estates use the same method as every other state.

  • Gross estate: everything owned or partly controlled at death, at fair market value. Cash, securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities and business interests all count.
  • Taxable estate: the gross estate minus allowed deductions such as debts, administration costs and bequests to a surviving spouse or qualified charity. Some operating businesses and farms may be valued lower if they qualify.
  • Lifetime gifts: taxable gifts made since 1977 are added before the tax is computed.
  • Credit: the tax is then reduced by the available unified credit.

Because mortgages are deductible, a heavily financed house counts for less than its market price. Spouses sometimes file even when no tax is due, because the return is how a surviving spouse claims the unused exemption through portability. If you are unsure whether a Form 706 applies, ask a tax professional, since the test counts gifts as well as the estate.

sections.h2: How the federal threshold has changed
sections.html:
The big jump came in 2018. For deaths in 2017 the IRS table lists $5,490,000, and for 2018 it lists $11,180,000. It has risen every year since, to $11,400,000 for 2019, $13,610,000 for 2024 and $15,000,000 for 2026.

Earlier years run from $5,000,000 for 2011 up through $5,450,000 for 2016. If your family read about the old limits, those numbers may no longer apply. Match the year of death to the IRS table before deciding whether a return is needed. The table also covers 2012 through 2015 for an older death.

sections.h2: How a Texas house passes to heirs
sections.html:
Which route fits depends on two things: whether a will exists and whether a judge has to oversee the process. Every route leaves a trail in the county clerk's records.

  • Probating a will: the application is due within four years of death, though a court may take a late one for good cause.
  • Muniment of title: suits an estate whose only debts are liens on the land. The order and the will get filed in the county of the land.
  • Small estate affidavit (Estates Code Chapter 205): a court-approved shortcut for estates at or under $75,000 before homestead and exempt property.
  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement left with the clerk. No law makes a buyer or lender accept it.
  • Transfer on death deed: moves land outside probate if recorded while the owner is alive.

The conditions are no will, no administration underway, enough assets to cover debts, and every heir in agreement. A judge must sign off.

This shortcut cannot carry real property unless it is a homestead going to a spouse or minor children. It also requires two disinterested witnesses, a waiting month after death, and no pending or granted petition for a personal representative. The homestead copy goes on record.

sections.h2: Which deed an heir needs to sell
sections.html:
Each route produces a different document, and the title company asks for the one that matches.

  • Transfer on death deed: a recorded affidavit of death with the certificate.
  • Administered estate: the executor's or administrator's deed.
  • Muniment of title: the order plus the will.
  • No court action: an affidavit of heirship.

A county will not rewrite the old deed to add heirs. The recorded instrument is what carries title forward. Ask the clerk what it charges to record.

sections.h2: Property tax on an inherited house
sections.html:
Probate does not pause the tax clock. On every January 1 a lien attaches for that year's taxes, penalties and interest, regardless of who ends up with title.

  • Billing starts around October 1 and delinquency begins February 1.
  • Late charges begin the day after January 31, and the penalty climbs through the summer.
  • If an heir is missing from the recorded deed, the exemption claim still works with four papers: an ownership affidavit, the death certificate, a utility bill and any court record citation.
  • In some cases a surviving spouse aged 55 or older inherits the over-65 exemption.

An heir who keeps the house and qualifies also gets the yearly appraisal cap on homesteads.

sections.h2: What makes a will valid for probate?
sections.html:
Expect a will to be written, signed and witnessed. A will in the maker's own handwriting, called holographic, needs no witnesses.

The probate court for the decedent's home county usually takes the application. A different tool, the enhanced life estate deed (called a Lady Bird deed), lets the owner keep full power to sell or borrow, although no official form exists.

sections.h2: First steps for heirs of a Texas house
sections.html:
Find out which route the estate will take, because that decides which document the title company needs. Locate any will, the death certificate and the latest deed.

  • Phone the appraisal district to learn what exemption the house carries now and whether a fresh application is due.
  • Find out from the county tax office if this year's bill is paid and what a payoff would cost.
  • Get from the county clerk a list of everything recorded against the property, liens included.
  • Keep the house insured and the utilities on while title is sorted out.

If the estate is large enough that the federal threshold might matter, bring in an accountant early, since the tax test counts lifetime gifts along with the house.

At closing, the sale price pays the mortgage, tax and recorded liens first, and the heirs share what is left under whatever route governs the estate. Line up the recorded deed, payoffs and tax statement before you accept an offer.

Federal rules govern income tax on a gain and gift tax, and a tax professional can answer those. Locally, ask the tax office for a payoff and the clerk for copies of what is recorded. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval, though the title paperwork above is still required.

faqs.q: Is there still a Texas inheritance tax?
faqs.a: There is none today. A 2015 law, Senate Bill 752, wiped out the state inheritance tax in Tax Code Chapter 211 beginning September 1, 2015.

faqs.q: At what estate size does a 2026 death trigger a federal return?
faqs.a: The figure is $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths, compared with $13,990,000 for 2025. Cross that line and a return is required; it is not a tax percentage.

faqs.q: Who pays the tax bill on a house that came through an estate?
faqs.a: Yes. The yearly lien sticks to the property on January 1, so the bill follows the house to whoever holds title.

faqs.q: How long after a death can a will be probated?
faqs.a: Generally four years after the death. After that, a court may still accept the application if it finds a good reason.

faqs.q: Is probate always needed before an heir can sell?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed in life, probate is avoided, and simpler estates may use a muniment of title or small estate affidavit. Your title company has the final say on what it will insure.
